statute: Madrid Agreement (1891) and Madrid Protocol (1989), administered by WIPO
title: Madrid System for the International Registration of Marks (Madrid Agreement and Protocol)
content:
The Madrid System lets a trade mark owner apply for protection in several member countries through one international application filed via the office of origin, in one language and with one set of fees, administered by WIPO.

Key mechanics relevant to Ayurvedic brands:
1. Basic mark: an international registration depends on a 'basic' application or registration in the office of origin (for Indian applicants, the Indian Trade Marks Registry). If the basic mark is refused, withdrawn or cancelled within five years of the international registration date, the international registration can fall with it ('central attack').
2. Designation: the applicant designates the member countries where protection is sought; each designated office examines the mark under its own national law and may issue a provisional refusal.
3. Territorial reach: protection is limited to designated members. A mark that implies a curative claim or is descriptive of a herb may be refused in a designated country under that country's law.
4. Practical link: an Indian brand should first secure the Indian basic mark (see Trade Marks Act provisions in this corpus), then decide export markets before designating.

This is a short curated summary, not the treaty text.
